claim: Phase response curves (PRCs) quantify how a neuron transforms input to output by spike timing.
source: Phase response curves (PRCs) quantify how a neuron transforms input to output by spike timing.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about PRCs that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: PRCs exhibit strong firing-rate adaptation.
source: PRCs exhibit strong firing-rate adaptation, but its mechanism and relevance for network output are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental observations and citations in the literature.

claim: The mechanism and relevance for network output of PRC firing-rate adaptation are poorly understood.
source: PRCs exhibit strong firing-rate adaptation, but its mechanism and relevance for network output are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the literature review.

claim: Rate adaptation of PRCs is caused by rate-dependent subthreshold membrane potentials efficiently regulating the activation of Na+ channels.
source: Using our Purkinje cell (PC) model, we demonstrate that the rate adaptation is caused by rate-dependent subthreshold membrane potentials efficiently regulating the activation of Na+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data from the PC model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in PRC cause oscillations and spike correlations only at high firing rates.
source: The changes in PRC cause oscillations and spike correlations only at high firing rates.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data showing rate-dependent oscillations.

claim: The causal role of the PRC is confirmed using a simpler coupled oscillator network model.
source: The causal role of the PRC is confirmed using a simpler coupled oscillator network model.
evidence: This is supported by simulations of the coupled oscillator model presented in the manuscript.

claim: This mechanism enables transient oscillations between fast-spiking neurons that thereby form PC assemblies.
source: This mechanism enables transient oscillations between fast-spiking neurons that thereby form PC assemblies.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data showing transient correlations.

claim: Rate adaptation of PRCs can spatio-temporally organize the PC input to cerebellar nuclei.
source: Our work demonstrates that rate adaptation of PRCs can spatio-temporally organize the PC input to cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results and their implications.

claim: The PRC determines the potential of network synchronization.
source: Consequently, the PRC determines the potential of network synchronization (Ermentrout et al., 2001; Ermentrout et al., 2008; Gutkin et al., 2005; Smeal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: In cerebellar Purkinje cells, their phase responses to weak stimuli at low firing rates are small and surprisingly flat.
source: In cerebellar Purkinje cells (PCs), their phase responses to weak stimuli at low firing rates are small and surprisingly flat.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the literature.

claim: With increased rates, responses in later phases become phase-dependent, with earlier onset-phases and gradually increasing peak amplitudes.
source: With increased rates, responses in later phases become phase-dependent, with earlier onset-phases and gradually increasing peak amplitudes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the literature.

claim: This PRC property has never been theoretically replicated or explained.
source: This PRC property has never been theoretically replicated or explained (Couto et al., 2015; Phoka et al., 2010), nor has its effect on synchronizing spike outputs been explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: The effect of PRC rate adaptation on synchronizing spike outputs has not been explored.
source: This PRC property has never been theoretically replicated or explained (Couto et al., 2015; Phoka et al., 2010), nor has its effect on synchronizing spike outputs been explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: High-frequency oscillations caused by reciprocal inhibition have been observed in many regions of the brain, including the cortex, cerebellum and hippocampus.
source: On the circuit level, high-frequency oscillations caused by reciprocal inhibition have been observed in many regions of the brain, including the cortex, cerebellum and hippocampus (Bartos et al., 2002; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Cheron et al., 2004; de Solages et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claim: All previous abstract and detailed PC models failed to replicate the experimentally observed rate adaptation of PRCs.
source: All previous abstract and detailed PC models failed to replicate the experimentally observed rate adaptation of PRCs (Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006; Couto et al., 2015; De Schutter and Bower, 1994; Khaliq et al., 2003; Phoka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: When the PC model fires at 12 Hz, responses (phase advances) to weak stimuli are small and nearly flat for the whole ISI.
source: When the PC model fires at 12 Hz, responses (phase advances) to weak stimuli are small and nearly flat for the whole ISI (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Only at a very narrow late phase do the responses become phase-dependent and slightly increased at 12 Hz firing rate.
source: Only at a very narrow late phase do the responses become phase-dependent and slightly increased.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data in Figure 1.

claim: With increased rates, the responses remain small and flat during early phases.
source: With increased rates, the responses remain small and flat during early phases.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Later phase-dependent peaks gradually become larger with increased firing rates.
source: However, later phase-dependent peaks gradually become larger (Figure 1C), with onset shifted to earlier phases (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The peak of PRCs became saturated at ~0.06 at high rates in agreement with experiments under the same stimulus conditions.
source: In agreement with experiments under the same stimulus conditions (Phoka et al., 2010), the peak of PRCs finally became saturated at ~0.06 at high rates.
evidence: This is supported by both simulation data and experimental citation.

claim: The relationship between normalized PRC peaks and rates can be fitted by the Boltzman function and matches experimental data.
source: The relationship between normalized PRC peaks and rates can be fitted by the Boltzman function and matches experimental data (Figure 1C, fitted with 1/ (1 + e−(rate−a)/b), a = 49.1, b = 26.4 in the model versus a = 44.1 and b = 20.5 in experiments Couto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by fitting simulation data and comparing to experimental data.

claim: PRCs in the PC model show similar rate adaption with inhibitory stimuli (phase delay).
source: PRCs in our model show similar rate adaption with inhibitory stimuli (phase delay, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: This form of rate adaptive PRCs requires the presence of a dendrite in the PC model.
source: This form of rate adaptive PRCs requires the presence of a dendrite in the PC model (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but the dendrite can be passive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data comparing models with and without dendrites.

claim: The dendrite can be passive for rate adaptive PRCs.
source: This form of rate adaptive PRCs requires the presence of a dendrite in the PC model (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but the dendrite can be passive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data with passive dendrites.

claim: Increasing stimulus amplitude consistently shifts onset-phases of phase-dependent peaks to the left and increases their amplitudes.
source: Increasing stimulus amplitude consistently shifts onset-phases of phase-dependent peaks to the left and increases their amplitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The facilitation of Na+ currents relative to K+ currents, due to elevated subthreshold membrane potentials at high rates, underlies the rate adaptation of PRCs.
source: We examined how spike properties vary with firing rates and find that the facilitation of Na+ currents relative to K+ currents, due to elevated subthreshold membrane potentials at high rates, underlies the rate adaptation of PRCs.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of simulation data and experimental data.

claim: Subthreshold membrane potential levels are significantly elevated at high firing rates.
source: As confirmed by re-analyzing in vitro somatic membrane potential recordings (shared by Ede Rancz and Michael Häusser Rancz and Häusser, 2010), subthreshold membrane potential levels are significantly elevated at high firing rates, but spike thresholds rise only slightly with rates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by re-analysis of experimental data and simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Spike thresholds rise only slightly with rates.
source: As confirmed by re-analyzing in vitro somatic membrane potential recordings (shared by Ede Rancz and Michael Häusser Rancz and Häusser, 2010), subthreshold membrane potential levels are significantly elevated at high firing rates, but spike thresholds rise only slightly with rates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by re-analysis of experimental data and simulation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ISI phase where Na+ activation threshold is crossed shifts to earlier phases with increasing rates.
source: This means that the ISI phase where Na+ activation threshold (~ −55 mV for 0.5% activation in PCs Khaliq et al., 2003; Zang et al., 2018) is crossed shifts to earlier phases with increasing rates.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on membrane potentials and Na+ activation threshold.

claim: Larger phase ranges of membrane potentials are above the Na+ activation threshold at high rates.
source: Consequently, larger phase ranges of membrane potentials are above the threshold at high rates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: During early phases of all firing rates, membrane potentials are distant from the Na+ activation threshold of the Na+ channels.
source: During early phases of all firing rates, membrane potentials are distant from the Na+ activation threshold of the Na+ channels (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The depolarizations to weak stimuli fail to activate sufficient transient and resurgent Na+ channels to speed up voltage trajectories during early phases.
source: The depolarizations to weak stimuli fail to activate sufficient transient and resurgent Na+ channels to speed up voltage trajectories (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phase advances in early phases are small and flat.
source: Consequently, phase advances in early phases are small and flat.
evidence: This is a consequence inferred from the Na+ channel activation data.

claim: At later phases, membrane potentials gradually approach and surpass the Na+ activation threshold.
source: At later phases, membrane potentials gradually approach and surpass the Na+ activation threshold.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data in Figure 2.

claim: Stimulus-evoked depolarizations activate more Na+ channels to speed up trajectories at later phases.
source: Stimulus-evoked depolarizations activate more Na+ channels to speed up trajectories in return.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between membrane potential and Na+ channel activation.

claim: Phase advances become large and phase-dependent at later phases.
source: Therefore, phase advances become large and phase- (actually voltage-) dependent.
evidence: This is a consequence inferred from the Na+ channel activation dynamics.

claim: High-rate-corresponding elevated membrane potentials have larger slopes at the foot of the Na+ activation curve.
source: Because high-rate-corresponding elevated membrane potentials have larger slopes at the foot of the Na+ activation curve, the same ∆V activates more Na+ channels and, in addition to the normalization, contributes to larger PRC peaks at high rates (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The same ∆V activates more Na+ channels at high rates and contributes to larger PRC peaks.
source: Because high-rate-corresponding elevated membrane potentials have larger slopes at the foot of the Na+ activation curve, the same ∆V activates more Na+ channels and, in addition to the normalization, contributes to larger PRC peaks at high rates (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Stimulus-evoked depolarizations also increase outward currents, but this increase is smaller than that of inward currents due to the high activation threshold of K+ currents in PCs.
source: Under all conditions (except phase = 0.2, 162 Hz), stimulus-evoked depolarizations also increase outward currents, but this increase is smaller than that of inward currents (mainly Na+) due to the high activation threshold of K+ currents (mainly Kv3) in PCs (Martina et al., 2003; Zang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and citations about K+ current properties.

claim: As the stimulus becomes stronger, the required pre-stimulus membrane potential (phase) to reach Na+ activation threshold is lowered.
source: As the stimulus becomes stronger, it triggers larger depolarizations and the required pre-stimulus membrane potential (phase) to reach Na+ activation threshold is lowered.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between stimulus strength and membrane potential dynamics.

claim: Increasing the stimulus amplitude not only increases PRC peaks, but also shifts the onset-phases of phase-dependent responses to the left.
source: Thus, increasing the stimulus amplitude not only increases PRC peaks, but also shifts the onset-phases of phase-dependent responses to the left (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the absence of a dendrite, the larger amplitude spike is followed by a stronger afterhyperpolarization that deactivates K+ currents allowing for an earlier depolarization in the ISI, resulting in a completely different PRC.
source: In the absence of a dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the larger amplitude spike is followed by a stronger afterhyperpolarization (Zang et al., 2018) that deactivates K+ currents allowing for an earlier depolarization in the ISI, resulting in a completely different PRC.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and citation.

claim: The critical role of subthreshold membrane potentials in shaping PRC profiles is not specific to the PC.
source: We further confirmed that the critical role of subthreshold membrane potentials in shaping PRC profiles is not specific to the PC by manipulating PRCs in a modified Traub model (Ermentrout et al., 2001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and accompanying text).
evidence: This is supported by simulations of the modified Traub model.

claim: Axon collateral contacts between PCs exist in adult mice.
source: Although axon collateral contacts between PCs were originally described to exist only in juvenile mice (Watt et al., 2009), recent work demonstrated their existence also in adult mice (Witter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: When the average cellular rate is 116 Hz, PCs in the network tend to fire within interspaced clusters with time intervals of ~6 ms.
source: When the average cellular rate is 116 Hz, PCs in the network tend to fire within interspaced clusters with time intervals of ~6 ms (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Individual PCs do not fire within every cluster.
source: However, individual PCs do not fire within every cluster.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data in Figure 3B.

claim: Spikes in the network show intermittent pairwise synchrony on the population level rather than spike-to-spike synchrony.
source: Therefore, spikes in the network show intermittent pairwise synchrony on the population level rather than spike-to-spike synchrony (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The network oscillates at a frequency of ~175 Hz based on the power spectrum.
source: Based on the power spectrum, the network oscillates at a frequency of ~175 Hz (inverse of the cluster interval,~6 ms), which is independent of cellular firing rates (116 Hz in red and 70 Hz in blue, Figure 3D), because oscillation frequency is mainly determined by synaptic properties (Brunel and Hakim, 1999; Brunel and Wang, 2003; de Solages et al., 2008; Maex and De Schutter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3D and citations.

claim: Oscillation frequency is independent of cellular firing rates.
source: Based on the power spectrum, the network oscillates at a frequency of ~175 Hz (inverse of the cluster interval,~6 ms), which is independent of cellular firing rates (116 Hz in red and 70 Hz in blue, Figure 3D), because oscillation frequency is mainly determined by synaptic properties (Brunel and Hakim, 1999; Brunel and Wang, 2003; de Solages et al., 2008; Maex and De Schutter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data and citations.

claim: Oscillation frequency is mainly determined by synaptic properties.
source: Based on the power spectrum, the network oscillates at a frequency of ~175 Hz (inverse of the cluster interval,~6 ms), which is independent of cellular firing rates (116 Hz in red and 70 Hz in blue, Figure 3D), because oscillation frequency is mainly determined by synaptic properties (Brunel and Hakim, 1999; Brunel and Wang, 2003; de Solages et al., 2008; Maex and De Schutter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: When cellular firing rates increase from 70 Hz to 116 Hz, the power of high-frequency oscillations significantly increases and the peak becomes sharper.
source: When cellular firing rates increase from 70 Hz to 116 Hz, the power of high-frequency oscillations significantly increases and the peak becomes sharper.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When individual PCs fire at low rates (10 Hz), the network fails to generate high-frequency oscillations and each PC fires independently.
source: When individual PCs fire at low rates (10 Hz), the network fails to generate high-frequency oscillations and each PC fires independently, as evidenced by the flat power spectrum (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When PCs fire at 70 Hz and 116 Hz, two significant side peaks can be observed in the CCGs in addition to positive central peaks.
source: When PCs fire at 70 Hz and 116 Hz, in addition to positive central peaks, two significant side peaks can be observed in the CCGs, suggesting correlated spikes with 0 ms-time lag and ~6 ms-time lag.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Amplitudes of the CCG peaks increase with cellular firing rates and disappear when they are low (10 Hz).
source: Amplitudes of the peaks increase with cellular firing rates and disappear when they are low (10 Hz).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When PCs fire with low to moderate CV of ISIs, they show loose spike-to-spike synchrony at high rates.
source: When PCs fire with low to moderate CV of ISIs, they show loose spike-to-spike synchrony at high rates, and the power peak increases with cellular firing rates.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: High-frequency oscillations were never observed for low cellular firing rates.
source: High-frequency oscillations were never observed for low cellular firing rates (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data.

claim: With high CV of ISIs, spikes are jittered and the loose spike synchrony is disrupted.
source: With high CV of ISIs, spikes are jittered and the loose spike synchrony is disrupted (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Small spiking irregularity supports high-frequency oscillations.
source: Our results show that small spiking irregularity supports high-frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Within the ranges of experimentally reported synaptic conductance and connection radius, the network generates robust high-frequency oscillations.
source: Within the ranges of experimentally reported synaptic conductance and connection radius (de Solages et al., 2008; Orduz and Llano, 2007; Watt et al., 2009; Witter et al., 2016), the network generates robust high-frequency oscillations (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data and citations.

claim: Increasing the conductance of inhibitory synapses or their connection radius increases the power of high-frequency oscillations and make the power spectrum sharper.
source: In addition, we find that increasing the conductance of inhibitory synapses or their connection radius increases the power of high-frequency oscillations and make the power spectrum sharper.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The correlation between PC spikes is strong under conditions of low to moderate spiking irregularity, high cellular firing rate, high synaptic conductance, and large connection radius.
source: Together, our simulation data suggest that the correlation between PC spikes is strong under conditions of low to moderate spiking irregularity, high cellular firing rate, high synaptic conductance, and large connection radius.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Decreasing PRC size leads to weaker oscillations and can even cause weaker oscillations at higher spike rates.
source: This is supported by the effect of PRC size on oscillations: decreasing its size leads to weaker oscillations and can even cause weaker oscillations at higher spike rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the coupled oscillator network, the oscillation power shows a firing rate dependence similar to that of the complex PC network.
source: In such a coupled oscillator network, the oscillation power shows a firing rate dependence similar to that of the complex PC network (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The firing rate adaptation of the PRC is sufficient to cause firing-rate-dependent oscillations.
source: This finding demonstrates that the firing rate adaptation of the PRC is sufficient to cause firing-rate-dependent oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the coupled oscillator model simulations.

claim: Networks simulated with fixed PRC peak amplitudes show power spectra that are very similar to that obtained with the actual PRC.
source: Networks simulated with fixed PRC peak amplitudes show power spectra (Figure 5C,D) that are very similar to that obtained with the actual PRC (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: The ratio of flat part width to peak width of the firing rate dependent PRC causes the rate dependence of high-frequency oscillations.
source: In conclusion, the ratio of flat part width to peak width of the firing rate dependent PRC causes the rate dependence of high-frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the coupled oscillator model simulations.

claim: At low firing rates the dominant flat part suppresses the coupling between oscillators.
source: At low firing rates the dominant flat part suppresses the coupling between oscillators.
evidence: This is inferred from the coupled oscillator model results.

claim: At high firing rates the coupling increases during the late peak and synchronizes the oscillators.
source: At high firing rates the coupling increases during the late peak and synchronizes the oscillators, but the strength of oscillation does not depend on peak amplitude in this network.
evidence: This is inferred from the coupled oscillator model results.

claim: The strength of oscillation does not depend on peak amplitude in the coupled oscillator network.
source: At high firing rates the coupling increases during the late peak and synchronizes the oscillators, but the strength of oscillation does not depend on peak amplitude in this network.
evidence: This is supported by the coupled oscillator model simulations.

claim: At low basal rates, there are no correlations between spikes.
source: At low basal rates, there are no correlations between spikes.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both 0 ms-time lag and 6 ms-time lag correlations start to increase ~250 ms after the onset of simulations when the cellular firing rate increases.
source: Both correlations start to increase ~250 ms after the onset of simulations when the cellular firing rate increases.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Correlations decrease again when the cellular rates drop, closely following rate changes.
source: Closely following rate changes, they decrease again when the cellular rates drop.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Axon collateral-caused spike correlations can be achieved transiently to transmit a correlation code conjunctive with temporal cellular firing rate increases.
source: It demonstrates that axon collateral-caused spike correlations can be achieved transiently to transmit a correlation code conjunctive with temporal cellular firing rate increases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the network simulation results.

claim: Spike correlations still become larger for the subgroup of PCs showing increased cellular rates, despite a slight decrease of the correlation amplitude when more cells decrease their spike rates.
source: Spike correlations still become larger for the subgroup of PCs showing increased cellular rates, despite a slight decrease of the correlation amplitude when more cells decrease their spike rates (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The spiking in PCs with decreased firing rates is not correlated.
source: Moreover, the spiking in PCs with decreased firing rates is not correlated (Figure 6F), nor is it correlated with oscillating increased-rate PCs (Figure 6G), making the assembly formation specific to fast spiking PCs.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Spiking in PCs with decreased firing rates is not correlated with oscillating increased-rate PCs.
source: Moreover, the spiking in PCs with decreased firing rates is not correlated (Figure 6F), nor is it correlated with oscillating increased-rate PCs (Figure 6G), making the assembly formation specific to fast spiking PCs.
evidence: This is supported by network simulation data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Assembly formation is specific to fast spiking PCs.
source: Moreover, the spiking in PCs with decreased firing rates is not correlated (Figure 6F), nor is it correlated with oscillating increased-rate PCs (Figure 6G), making the assembly formation specific to fast spiking PCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the network simulation results.

claim: A population of PCs with increased spike rates can form a correlated assembly that will strongly affect downstream neurons even when it is surrounded by non-correlated neighboring PCs with decreased spike rates.
source: The results suggest that a population of PCs with increased spike rates can form a correlated assembly that will strongly affect downstream neurons even when it is surrounded by non-correlated neighboring PCs with decreased spike rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the network simulation results.

claim: Cerebellar PCs exhibit a transition from small, phase-independent responses to large, phase-dependent type-I responses with increasing rates.
source: Cerebellar PCs exhibit a transition from small, phase-independent responses to large, phase-dependent type-I responses with increasing rates (Couto et al., 2015; Phoka et al., 2010), but the mechanism was unknown (Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006; Couto et al., 2015; De Schutter and Bower, 1994; Khaliq et al., 2003; Phoka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The mechanism of the transition from small, phase-independent responses to large, phase-dependent type-I responses with increasing rates was unknown.
source: Cerebellar PCs exhibit a transition from small, phase-independent responses to large, phase-dependent type-I responses with increasing rates (Couto et al., 2015; Phoka et al., 2010), but the mechanism was unknown (Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006; Couto et al., 2015; De Schutter and Bower, 1994; Khaliq et al., 2003; Phoka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: This work reproduces and explains the experimentally observed rate adaptation of PRCs.
source: This work reproduces and explains the experimentally observed rate adaptation of PRCs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the work's contribution.

claim: The slight increase of PRCs in the very narrow late phase in the model at low rate may be annihilated by noise in spontaneously firing neurons.
source: Note that the slight increase of PRCs in the very narrow late phase in our model (low rate, Figure 1B) may be annihilated by noise in spontaneously firing neurons (Couto et al., 2015; Phoka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about why experimental data might differ from model predictions.

claim: In both pyramidal neurons and PCs, spike rates cause significant variation of the subthreshold membrane potential during the ISI.
source: In both pyramidal neurons and PCs, spike rates cause significant variation of the subthreshold membrane potential during the ISI (Rancz and Häusser, 2010; Tsubo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In PCs, the main K+ current is high-threshold activated.
source: In PCs, the main K+ current is high-threshold activated (Martina et al., 2003; Zang et al., 2018); therefore, depolarization-facilitated Na+ currents dominate, causing larger normalized PRCs at high rates (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations and simulation data.

claim: Depolarization-facilitated Na+ currents dominate in PCs, causing larger normalized PRCs at high rates.
source: In PCs, the main K+ current is high-threshold activated (Martina et al., 2003; Zang et al., 2018); therefore, depolarization-facilitated Na+ currents dominate, causing larger normalized PRCs at high rates (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of K+ and Na+ currents and supported by simulation data.

claim: This facilitation may be further boosted in PCs by enhanced excitability, such as SK2 down-regulation reducing the AHP and elevating subthreshold membrane potentials.
source: This facilitation may be further boosted in PCs by enhanced excitability, such as SK2 down-regulation reducing the AHP and elevating subthreshold membrane potentials (Grasselli et al., 2020; Ohtsuki and Hansel, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: Previous PC models included low-threshold-activated K+ currents, which counteract facilitated Na+ currents.
source: Previous PC models (Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006; Couto et al., 2015; De Schutter and Bower, 1994; Khaliq et al., 2003; Phoka et al., 2010) included low-threshold-activated K+ currents, which counteract facilitated Na+ currents.
evidence: This is a statement about previous models supported by citations.

claim: In the original Traub model, slow deactivation of K+ currents and consequent hyperpolarization synergistically reduce the normalized PRC peaks at high rates.
source: In the original Traub model, slow deactivation of K+ currents and consequent hyperpolarization synergistically reduce the normalized PRC peaks at high rates (Ermentrout et al., 2001; Gutkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on the Traub model.

claim: By minimally modifying the Traub model, elevated subthreshold membrane potentials generate larger normalized PRC peaks at high rates.
source: By minimally modifying the Traub model, elevated subthreshold membrane potentials generate larger normalized PRC peaks at high rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rate-dependent synchrony in the cerebellum has been demonstrated for Golgi cells but not, as yet, for PCs.
source: Rate-dependent synchrony in the cerebellum has been demonstrated for Golgi cells (van Welie et al., 2016) but not, as yet, for PCs.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of experimental evidence supported by citation.

claim: In the work of de Solages et al., 2008, units with lower average rates (<10 Hz) did not exhibit significant correlations between neighboring PCs, for unknown reasons.
source: In the work of de Solages et al., 2008, units with lower average rates (<10 Hz) did not exhibit significant correlations between neighboring PCs, for unknown reasons.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations from a cited study.

claim: The lack of correlations at low rates can be explained by the small flat PRCs at low rates.
source: This can be explained by the small flat PRCs at low rates.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the model results to experimental observations.

claim: When the PRC is constantly 0 (equivalent to disconnection), no correlations can be achieved.
source: Under extreme conditions, when the PRC is constantly 0 (equivalent to disconnection), no correlations can be achieved (Figures 3–6).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: The experimental oscillation power increased by the application of WIN 55,212–2, which was intended to suppress background excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Additionally, the experimental oscillation power increased by the application of WIN 55,212–2, which was intended to suppress background excitatory and inhibitory synapses (de Solages et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations from a cited study.

claim: The increased power could be due to more regular spiking after inhibiting the activity of background synapses.
source: The increased power could be due to more regular spiking after inhibiting the activity of background synapses (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a speculation connecting experimental observations to model predictions.

claim: The increased power could also be caused by increased spike rates, because WIN 55,212–2 also blocks P/Q type Ca2+ channels and consequently P/Q type Ca2+-activated K+ currents, to increase spike rates.
source: However, it could also be caused by increased spike rates (Figure 4A), because this agent also blocks P/Q type Ca2+ channels and consequently P/Q type Ca2+-activated K+ currents, to increase spike rates (Fisyunov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation and model predictions.

claim: Enhanced oscillations have been observed in calcium-binding protein gene KO mice, which have significantly higher simple spike rates.
source: Similarly, enhanced oscillations have also been observed in calcium-binding protein gene KO mice, which have significantly higher simple spike rates (Cheron et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: The rate-dependent correlations observed in this study are different from those reported previously by de la Rocha et al., 2007.
